B. Is this measure already running in City of Helsinki (or in the HUS university hospital area that treats its patients)?
A. Does recent evidence support the size of effect we assume: does this measure shorten the time from first symptom to treatment start for lung cancer patients, and by how many days?
Measure: Reflex molecular testing ordered by pathology. The pathologist starts the biomarker panel (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, PD-L1, NGS) as soon as non-small cell lung cancer is seen, without waiting for the oncologist to order it. The result now decides treatment at every stage: osimertinib or alectinib after surgery, durvalumab or osimertinib after chemoradiotherapy in stage III, and the first drug in advanced disease.
effect_summary_en: A 2026 systematic review of 20 NSCLC studies reports reflex testing shortened time to treatment by 1–44 days.
supported_en: Reflex testing shortens NSCLC time to treatment by 1–44 days (Future Oncology systematic review, 2026).
not_supported_en: No HUS or Finnish data on the ordering delay, so the 7-day gain locally is unverified.
in_use_summary_en: No public sign of reflex testing started by pathology at HUS. HUSLAB has offered an NGS panel with EGFR and ALK since March 2020, but no page says who orders it.
summary_en: HUS pages say biopsies are tested for molecular changes that guide treatment, with results in 2–3 weeks. HUSLAB has run an in-house NGS panel that includes EGFR and ALK since 30.3.2020. No page says the testing is started by pathology rather than ordered by the clinician. A 2026 systematic review (Future Oncology) found that reflex testing in non-small cell lung cancer cut time to treatment by 1–44 days, so our 7-day assumption fits inside that range, but no Finnish figure confirms it.
unanswered_en: Whether HUS pathologists already order the panel automatically was not stated on any page found.
